AT the present moment the French Govern -
Meat and the French nation occupy before
Europe a painfully humiliating position. They
have been dragged from under a degrading
despotism by the rough hand of war. They
have been despoiled of the profit for which
they had sold their liberty to a tyrant. Their
glory, which at least seemed to be a comfort to
them, has been trampled on in the red slough
of their many disastrous battle-fields. They
have suffeced everything a people could surfer
short of utter destruction, and they have come
out of the trial with scarcely anything of a
nation but the name, with no belief in any
old principle that has been proved in the past or
of any new principle from which hope can be de-
rived foT the future. Franoe,as represented in her
Assembly, is a disorganised mob, one portion of
Which struggles blindly and furiously against
another, whilst every section is alike without
Policy, imposer or force sufficient to do any
great work for the redemption of the nation.
In her eourts of justice a spectacle not quite
the same, but quite as disheartening, is exhi-
bited, and in the open day and before the eyes
of the world, M. JANVIER DE LA MOTTE is
justified and freed from even blame for acts
Which could only be committed or condoned
Where public morality or a public conscience
had ()eased to exist.

The insensate friends of property and order
in that country have recently boon busy in
Shaping a law for the extermination of the
International Society, without seeming to
Understand what this S Aiety is, or what
Means. What it has done, or what it may
Mean to do, inspires that ignorant terror,
Which in the past has so frequently led
to blind and brutal attempts at repression;
and which in the present will add to the
disgrace of France without in the least in-
creasing its safety. IL DuFaunE declares
that "the International is carrying on a
Propagandist war against property and
society," and he proposes to make the fact of
belonging to it, or to any similar society, an
eftenee against the public peace, punishable with
iraPrisouMent for not less than three months, or
more than two years, and a fine not exceeding
£4O, in addition to a loss of civil rights for five
Years. And if the accused should hold any
kind of olliee in the Society all these penalties
are to be doubled. The Assembly, as a matter
of course, passed this Bill. Bourbonists, 80.
napartists, Iturals, all those frantic friends
"Property and order," who have boon
saving society" for the last half-century,
carried it triumphantly by 501 votes over a
kinority of 104, and it is to be hoped that
for a time at least the fears of the respectable
°lasses in Franco will be somewhat quieted.
• Rnglish working men will have no trouble
111 understanding what this attack on their
brethren in France means. It means the
complete Suppression of the right of associa.

tion amongst working men. There is no single
purpose for which they can associate, either
connected with the political state of the
country, or with their social and industrial
condition as workers, which this abominable
law will not cover. Political societies, Trades
unions, all must go down before the powerful
range and sweep of its arm. Active politicians, as
well as trades unionists, will be made its
victims, and no mercy will be shown to men
amongst the working classes who ask for
political reforms, or who in any way attempt
to interfere in questions concerning the price
or rights of labour. The situation in France,
as far as working men are concerned, is very
serious. But though the right of public meet-
ing be denied, the power of conspiring will
remain, and there are few things more certain
than that this power will be exercised. What
all this may end in, it would be premature to
state here, but that working men will over
abandon their right to protect their interests
because the law unjustly interferes with thorn,
is what nobody can believe who has honestly
studied thole character, condition, and require-
ments.

Turning our eyes from France to England,
the same spirit in a feeble and almost ludicrous
way is at work. To silence the public
voice, to stifle public opinion, to hold in
cheek the enthusiasm of crowds, to out
off all ahem* of dimming any ques-
tion discomforting to our upper demi,'
the Park Bill of Mr, AYRTON was in-
troduced. A bold stroke, but it has not as
yet produced the intended effect; and as we
arc told that there is but one step from the sub-
lime to the ridiculous, this ambitions effort
of our great ComussiorrEn of WORKS and
BUILDINGS is followed by the closing up of the
"Hole-in-the-Wall," as a preventive to Re
publicanism, and to all other wildnesses of
political thought. It appears that the " Hole-

complaining:of the thing as a nuisance is too

and it is in itself most certainly contemptible in

magistrates, and other "pillars of the State"
in attempting shabby oppressions amongst the I

in one

wrote to the President of the Club, warning
him against the dangerous consequences of
defacing her MAJESTY'S property. It is true

2. By applying the provisions of the Act to

I have taken care that no injurious disclosure

So much for the proposed extension of the

that both parties should submit to arbitration
in manner prescribed. This gives the founda-

tration as Frovided by. Lord Si, LEONARD'S

Two years ago we tried to improve our working
condition, for at that time, and until this strike
took place, we were working between 70 and 80
hours per week. On the 10th of October, 1870,
a petition was sent to each master, asking them to
meet us at any 'time, and place it would be conve-
nient for them Within a fortnight. The anima
we got was 'a . notice posted on the gates of. the
workshops, intimating that any one who NM not
satisfied with. the way of 'working might. leave by
giving a Week's notice. This notice hed the de-
sired effect; for as we were not prepared to fight
a battle, no more was said at that time. Thus
the question dropped; but at the commencement
of this year, seeing all other trades getting the
nine hours conceded them, we again raised the
question, and on the 22nd of January we held a
general meeting to consider the steps to be taken,
but no resolutions were adopted. Our masters
heard of this, and they had
.a meeting the same
week, and took immediate action. Each of the
largest firms stopped one house or shop, and
thereby thowing one-sixth of the men out of
work to be a burden on the society, and to make
us afraid, under the pretence of slack trade. On
February the iith we held another meeting to
consider our position, and the action taken by the
/employers. Deputations were appointed from
each factory to wait upon their respective em-
ployers, but in this we were unsuccessful, for the
masters would not listen to their men; all we
could get from thorn was—do not come to us
again; we will not hesr you.; we will not be dic-
tated to as to hew we shall rule our Works. We
were willing and desirous to meet them to argue
our case inn friendly manner, but we could not
get anything from them by circular or deputation;
so we were compelled to give notice, and on the
10th of February we sent in a petition asking for
a limitation of 60 hours per week, and stating
that if it did not meet with their approval we
should cease to work on the 17th, and on that
day the gates were closed. I must here state that
all our work is piece work, so that by working
10 hours per week less we should be the losers,
and not the masters, for we are not asking any
advance on our present rate, and that alone is
quite sufficient to justify us for the small demands
made upon our late employers. I hesitate not in
saying that our request is one of the most reason-
able demands that has been made by any class or
body of 'men in this country, and just one half of
the employers said they were wiling to accept
the terms of the men, but they were bound not
to do so. Therefore it is a plain stubborn fact that
their only object is to crush our society, and
prevent us from enjoying the same benefits and
privileges our fellow tradesmen in England have
enjoyed for many years. The glass bottle makers

of Scotland have been too long in the gutter; the
time has come when we must lift ourselves up,
and take our position in the world equhl with
other" tradesmen, or else cut ourselves off from
society altogether. Fellow workmen, I appeal to
you for your sympathy and support ; this is the
fifth week of the strike; there are 250 men out,
and our funds only amounted to £1,200 to com.
mence with, so it will depend almost ' entirely
upon your generosity; this is a battle of right
against might, and we pledge, ourselves to return
the compliment when you stand rn. need if you
will come forward and assist xis in this time of
need.

A misunderstanding has for some time past ex-
isted between the Liverpool Cotton Brokers'
Association and the Cotton Spinners' Association
of Manchester, in the course of which some toler-
ably strong and outspoken expressions have been
used by both sides. The dispute arose in the first
instance from the publication in the newspapers of
some remarks made by the retiring president of
the Cotton Brokers' Association, to the afoot that
the standard of morality in` the cotton trade had
lately much improved, though it still was not so
high as it stood some years ago. On this report
appearing in the papers an "indignation" meeting
of the Association was held, and, after a fiery dis-
cussion, it was resolved that such publication was
a " breach of confidence" on the part of the mem-
ber who had given it to the papers, and a further
resolution was passed prohibiting any member from
supplying information to the newspapers. In spite,
however, of this resolution, short reports of the
proceedings at subsequent meetings appeared in
the papers, and excited displeasure among the
majority of the members.
The manufacturing department of the cotton
trade remains in a very depressed condition, and
this depression is, perhaps, more keenly felt in
Blackburn and East Lancashire than in any other,.
of the cotton-manufacturing districts. In Black-
burn and its environs it is the weaving branch of
the trade that is mainly carried on, and some idea
of the ill effects of the depression in the cloth
markets upon the district may be ha 4 wh,ett we

state that in Blackburn alono more cloth is
manufactured than in any other place in the
world.

The operatives are actively agitating the nine
hours' system, believing that its adoption, by les-
sening the rate Of production, will prove a remedy
for the present unsatisfactory state of things.
Several of the manufacturers have publicly come
to the aid of the operatives in carrying on the
agitation. Some important statistics . have been
put forward in support of the movement. It is
stated that from 1850 to 1868 the consumption of
cotton increased 78 per cent., while the hands em-
ployed increased only 21 per cent., and, further,
that if the nine hours system is adopted it will be
equivalent to the total stoppage of 33,000 looms in
the Blackburn district alone.

settle the dispute now existing between the masters
and the men. Meanwhile, the labourers receive
a vast amount of popular support, and every post
brings letters of sympathy and assistance from
various parts of the country.
TituusnAlr.—During the week the agricultural
labourers have boon holding open air meetings

with the view of extending the Union and collect-
ing funds for the relief of those out on strike.
The attendance is invariably good, and enthusiastic
demonstrations frequently occur in favour of the
movement. Sqmetimes as many as 70 members
are enrolled in the Union at the close of the

meetings. One of these gatherings was held at
Radford, Sewell, on Monday evening, and on
Tuesday there was a second at Tysoo, near Edge
Hills. The numbers present vary from 200 to
300 up to 800 and 900. With it few exceptions,
the farmers are bent upon resisting the demands of
the men, and seriously talk of a general lock out.
Many labourers have already received notices to
quit their cottages in consequence of their con-
nexion with the Union, or sympathy with thos3
out on strike. It is calculated that next week
there will be upwards of 400 men out of work, the
bulk of whom are fathers of large families.

articles.title: LEAMINGTON.
articles.text:
LEAMINGTON.

THE BRICK:MAKERS.

The operative brickmakers have returned to
work, having obtained their demand, Is. 6d. per
thousand for common bricks, and 23. for anything
out of the square. The price of bricks consequently
has advanced 23. a thousand. The operative house
painters we hear have already been promised
an advance of wages by 26 out of 40 of their
employers.

CAMBRIDG FL
TUE CARPENTEM AND BRICKLAYERS.

The carpenters and bricklayers have held
meetings in favour of the nine hours' movement,
and an advance of wages. The meetings have
been numerously attended, and at thorn resolutions
wore unanimously adopted. for 54 hours labour in a
week, with half-holiday on Saturdays, and a rate
of wage at CA. per hour. On Monday night last
the labourers held a meeting and resolved upon
demanding 4th per hour and working 54 hours per
week with a half-holiday on Saturdays. 'The

smiths have struck upon the time question
demanding 3} hours less labour in a week.

NOrrINGLIAM.
TILE FRAMEWORK KNITTERS.

The workmen of Nottingham, Hathern, and
Kirkby, in the Ribbed Top Framework Knitters'
branch have appealed to their employers for an
advance of wages, and being refused in every
attempt to settle the dispute by arbitration, are
cornpelled to strike. But they wish to state
their ease to the public, and leave it to
judge whether they arc justified in taking that
course. The workmen in the country have been
receiving only 7d. per dozen for the same article
that the workmen of Nottingham receive lOid,
for, and have been offered by the employers Bth
This the workmen object to, and why, they ask,
should the workmen in the country be compelled
to work at 21 per cent. less than the workmen in
Nottingham.
The workmen of Nottingham have made the
country case their case, and have ceased work to
help the country workmen to accomplish their
object, and to aid them in redeeming their rights;
for be it remembered the country workmen are
receiving, and the price offered by their employers
is a less price than they received 16 years ago;
and this, contrasted with the great increase of
every commodity they have to use, makes it a
thing almost impossible to live at the present
price of their work. They belong to the Organised
Trades of Nottingham, and having 221 men out
on strike, and their funds being small, they trust
that all trade societies -will render all the assist-
ance possible, to enable them to continue this
important struggle, and to keep their wives and
children from crying for broad ; for they:are de-
termined to hold out at whatever cost.

Subscriptions will be thankfully received, and
any information given by the committee at Mr. R.
Fuller's, Old English Gentleman, Moynell-street,
Nottingham.

WIGAN.
TDB MEMBERS AND THE TRADE.

A soiree, in connection with the Wigan Liberal
Working Mon's Club, was held in the Public Hall,
on Tuesday. Mr. K. Cornish, a working man, in
proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Woods, M.P.,
and Mr. Lancaster, M.P., expressed his satisfaction
with the Mines Regulation Bill, and Master an d
Servants Wages Act. Ho hoped that bpth Bills
would receive the support of the members. Ho
strongly denounced the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act of last Session, and told the members
that they promised at the last election
to support a Trades Union Bill, that
should place both master and workman on an
equality before the law. lie hoped they would
redeem that pledge by giving Mr. Vernon Harcourt
their support in his endeavours to get the Act
repealed. Mr. Woods, in reply, said they were
fully prepared to carry out, to the letter, all they
promised at the election.

articles.title: WEST YORKSHIRE. THE QUARRYMEN.
articles.text:
WEST YORKSHIRE.
THE QUARRYMEN.

The dispute which has prevailed for several
weeks now shows signs of coming to an end. At
Morley, the masters have advanced the wages of
strapplers and the boat workmen from 265. to 28s.
pot week, the hours of labour being 50i per
week.

articles.title: PONTYPRIDD. TILE TAFF VALE MINERS.
articles.text:
PONTYPRIDD.
TILE TAFF VALE MINERS.

At a large meeting of Taff Vale railway ser-
vants, held at Pontypridd, on Saturday, it was
agreed to press the company for another shilling a
week advance in wages for those men who have
been in the company's :_;ervice for two years and
upwards. They also resolved to continue an agi-
tation in favour of a limitation of hours of labour
to ten hours per day, or sixty hours per week. In
reference to this demand, the delegates who had
waited on Mr. Fisher, the manager of the com-
pany, reported that he had said that "they
should not have it as long as he was under the

articles.text:
company."

STOCKTON-ON-TEES.
THE JOURNEYMEN TAILOR.

The journeymen tailors of Stockton have sent a
circular to each employer in the town, desiring
that they will raise the present rate of payment
from 4d. to 41,d. per hour. They have likewise
sent a now wages bill with the circular, in which
the price on the " start " of most garments is raised
from 15 to 20 per cent. above the old prices. A.
meeting of employers has been held on the subject,
and they decided to ask the men for a fortnight's
more time that they might give the question their
fall consideration. Whilst asking for this exten-
sion of time, they intimated to the men that the
general feeling of the musters was to increase the
rate of wages above the amount now paid.

JARROW.
STRIKE OP SHIPBUILDERS' PkINTERS.

_
On Monday the whole of the painters in the
employment of Messrs. Palmer and Company, iron
-
shipbuilders, Jarrow, turned out on strike for an
advance in their wages. The painters were receiving
28s. per week, and they applied to their employers
for an increase of 28. per week in their wages.
The masters were willing to give one part of the
men 295. per week, and the skilful or superior men
308. per week. This arrangement did not suit the
men, and they accordingly turned out on strike
for 30s. per week.

LEEK.

THE LOCK-OtT IN THE BILK TEADE.

At a meeting of the Leek silk manufacturers,
hold on Saturday, a letter was read from the secre-
tary of the Twisters' Society, to the effect "that
the operative silk twisters were willing • that the
present suicidal struggle should be settled by arbi-
tration." The opinion of the meeting was thab
the masters were best able to settle a matter
relating to their own business, and the offer was
rejected.
A deputation of workmen waited upon the silk
manfacturers of Leek on Tuesday, and one of theca
proposed that the latter should give at once half
the advance originally asked, and consider as to
the other half at the end of two months. The
masters refused to entertain the proposal, and the
men withdrew, expressing their determination not
to resume work until an advance had Wm
conceded.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM. THE LETTIIIITRESS PRINTERS.
articles.text:
BIRMINGHAM.
THE LETTIIIITRESS PRINTERS.

A number of meetings of members of the Bir-
mingham branch of the Provincial Typographical
Association have been held during the past few
weeks, having for their object the memorialising of
the employers for a rise of wages. The branch is
moving with the express sanction of the Executive
at Manchester, as will be seen by the following
issued by the local secretary, Mr. Boodle :
"To the Letterpress Printers of Birmingham.
" GENnzum.r,—The question of the re-organisa-
tion of the jobbing trade, with the ultimate view ot
agitating for arise of wages to 30s. per week, having
been laid before the Executive Council at Man-
chester, I fun instructed to inform of the following
resolution, passed by the Board on the 21st.
ultimo :---‘ The Council regard with great satis-
faction the attempt now being made to improve
the position of the jobbing trade in 13irminglia0i,
and beg to assure the branch that they will render
all the aid in their power to carry such movement
to a successful issue. They therefore approve the
efforts making to re-organise the trade, and when
that re-organisation is complete, the Council vril/
enter into no other important engagements tilt
their energies have been devoted to an attempt to
improve the position of the jobbing trade in Bir-
mingham.'"

articles.title: PAINTEIIS.
articles.text:
THE PAINTEIIS.

A conference between master operative painters
was held on Friday evening, at Mr. Jos. Hillman's,
top of New street. The operatives had issued cir-
culars requesting their employers to give them an
increase of wages, and for a reduction of the
hours of labour. After considerable discussion,
the masters decided to give the men the advance
on their wages, and the men withdrew their re-
quest for shorter hours, the time still remaining
56i hours per week, as before.

LEEDS.
THE STRIKES IN THE FLAX AND FELT TRAVEg,
There does not appear to be a prospect a
early termination of the above disputes.

VW. FLAX TRADE.
By arrangement there was a meeting betweori
seven operatives and seven masters in the fk"
trade, at the Queen's Hotel, Leeds, on FrideY'
when the operatives proposed the nine ilore
system. They were requested to withdraw while
the masters considered the proposition, 101'1,1
their return the masters announced that they
come to this resolution: —"That the masters Wl°
resolved that they will open their mills on Sat'lt'
day morning at six o'clock; and with regard to the
increase of wages, they are prepared to make ell
addition upon present rates of remuneration, the
condition being that each employer arranges 'with
his own workpeople."
On Friday afternoon a meeting was bold at the
Assembly-rooms, when the workpeople refused the
terms offered, stating that they should- insist Wu
the nine hours programme.
The flax mills were re-opened on Saturday Alla
following mornings in accordance with the resolu:
tion of the employers adopted at the Qw3eo
Hotel on Friday, but very few hands availed them-
selves of the opportunity to return to work'
Daring the morning a mass meeting of the factory

operatives on strike was held on liolbeck Moor,
and it was resolved to remain out until the nino
hours system is adopted.
The flax operatives on strike at Leeds received
their second pay on Wednesday afternoon. The
Bum distributed was £354, against £240 last week.
Nearly 5,000 were relieved.

articles.title: THS FELT TRADE.
articles.text:
THS FELT TRADE.

On Thursday a meeting of a committee of the
felting trades was held. The delegates stated
that when the deputation waited upon the employ-
ers for the concession of the nine hours system
they were told that the employers could not
compete with the Rossendalo manufacturers if
they allowed the nine hours system. It had, how-
ever, been found that the operatives in the Rossen-
dale district were receiving from 10 to 20 per cent.
more wages than their brethren in Leeds, and,
moreover, that the work done by women in Leeds
WU the same as that executed by adult males in
the Lancashire districts.

13ROMSGROVE.
THE BUILDING TRADES.

A largely, attended meeting of carpenters, brick-
layers, masons, plumbers, and painters, and others
engaged in the building trades, was held at the
Green Dragon Inn, on Wednesday night, to con-
sider the present position of the trade with re.
spect to the rise of wages and shortening of hours
taking place in other towns. Mr. It. Prosser
presided. A discussion took place, and the fol-
lowing resolutions were proposed :—" That the
men work by the hour in future, instead of by
the day, as at present; that the rate of pay be
sixpence per hour for all skilled labour, and in
proportion for less skilled labour; and that work
cease at one o'clock on Saturday."

AN APPEAL TO THE TRADES UNION-
ISTS OF GREAT BRITAIN,
FELLow Woaxstzw,—The agricultural labourers
are rousing themselves and forming unions in al-
most every county in England., What will you
do to help them? They are, as a rule, almost en-
tirely ignorant of the A B C of trades unionism,
and those persons who are exerting themselves on
behalf of the labourers, appeal to you, the trades
unionists of Great Britain, for sympathy and sup-
port. We ask for copies of rules, for advice how
to proceed in the matter of getting the union
registered, &c. We will cheerfully pay any ex-
penses incurred, and willingly co-operate with all
other unions in every thing that tends to the bet-
tering of the workmen's condition.
Our union is the first great stop towards our
social and political freedom. Help us then for
the take of social and.political progress, and make
U$ your ever grateful brothers.
Wat. BANES.
36, Pon-street, Boston, Lincolnshire.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES.

BIMINI:MAX.—A conference of masters and
men in the painting trade, was held on Friday
night, at Mr. Hillman's, New-street, when, after
discussing the question of time, it was arranged
that the men adhere to tho present system—viz.,
661 hours a week.
BLDWORTIL—The miners employed at the
Charity and Ilawkesbury Collieries, Bedworth,
known RN the "bondsmen," have resumed work,
the masters having conceded their demand, which
warn that the hours of work should be reduced
from ton and a half to nine. The workmen known
as the "getters "—or hewers of coal—have now
given notice for a reduction of their working
hours from eight to seven, and it is believed that
on the expiration of the notice the masters will
accede to their request.
Ntarsairow.—On Friday a meeting of miners.
Val held at the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Nuneaton, to
consider what steps it would be advisable to take
to obtain a reduction of the hours of labour
The Chairman said that the notice which had been
given to their employeis had expired, and as the
litter had declined to concede their demands, he
trusted every man would remain on strike until
they did so. The masters had expressed their
willingnos t:e reduce the hours of work from ten to
nine, but he thought that no miner ought to work
more than eight hours a day. Some discussion
ensued as to the propriety of forming a miners'
association for the protection of labour, and it
was agreed that such a society should be estab-
lished. It was unanimously resolved to continuo
the strike until the miners' request is acceded to.
Monuy.—The strike among the quarrymen of
Morley continues. Some of the employers have
placardoil the town with the offer of 2s. asked for
but in the place of a reduction of two hours they
ask the men to work a half-hour more time than
before the strike. The men are determined not to
resume work on those conditions. The number on
strike is decreasing rapidly, the Men haying got
Work elsewhere,

DUNDEE.—The deputation from Leeds had a
, very friendly meeting with the Dundee
.Trade
Council. The deputation explained the position of
their constituents, stating that the strike rendered
the solicitation of subscriptions from those beyond
the immediate sphere of it necessary. The Council
resolved to form an organisation for the collection
of subscriptions, and at the same time expressed
entire sympathy with their movement.
DUDLEY.—On Saturday night a meeting was
held at the Hope Tavern, High-street, Dudley, in
order that local colliery engineers might have an
opportunity of forming a branch of the Amal-
gamated Association of Colliery Winders at
Prince's End. In furtherance of this, a deputation
aftended from the latter place and addressed the
meeting, which consisted of winders from the fol-
lowing collieries Park Lane, Corbyn's Hall,
Conegre, Buffery Lane, Newbury Lane, Prince of
Wales, and Messrs. Grazebrook and Astur,
Netherton. After hearing the deputation, it was
agreed to form a branch of the union, and also agi-
tate for the nine hours movement, pure and
simple.
KinKcAr.Dx. The floor-cloth operatives of
'Kirkcaldy struck on Saturday for the 51 hours
limit, having refused to accept the offer of 54
hours for a week's work, as offered by the
masters.

BRADFORD.—Tho machine woolcombers of Brad-
ford have held a meeting, and apptiinted a com-
mittee to 'assist the factory workers' short time
movement. Efforts are also to be made to organ-
ise a united movement with the view of securing
an advance of the wages of machine wool-
combers. The operative silk warp, skein, and
velvet dyers engaged in the dyeworks of Messrs.
Lister and Co., Manainghatn Mills, near Bradford
are to have their hours of labour reduced from 59
to 54 hours per week, to date from the 15th instant.
STAMFORD.—The question of the wages of
agricultural labourers in Lincolnshire is still in an
unsettled state. On some of the farms the men
are at work at the old wages, on other farms they
are bolding out for more money or less hours.
Some of the masters have tried to carry the day
with a high hand, and set the men at defiance,
which, as may very reasonably be supposed, has
only widened. the breach between them. Others
who have taken the matter more quietly, and
made some slight concessions, have not lost a man
for a single day.
WALSALL.—A meeting of the operatives in the
bridle cutting trade was held in the Temperance
Hall, Walsall, on Saturday: ' After hearing the re-
ports of the deputiesreromtho various factories, the
secretary was instructed to write to the employers
inviting thorn to a friendly conference. •
STOURBRIDGE.—A. meeting of the employds at
the Mersey Wheelworks, Stourbridge, was hold at
the Duke William Inn, Coventry Street, Stour-
bridge, on Saturday night, for the purpose of con-
sidering the desirability of adopting the nine
hours movement. It was unanimously resolved,
"That a memorial should be presented to Mr.
Thomas Parker, the proprietor of the works,
soliciting him te grant them the nine hours move-
ment, as a similar concession had been made to
the men employed in the Derby. works." A reply
was requested by the 23rd inst. The memorial
was signed by the Chairman and the whole of the
members present.
SLINOBBY.—A second mooting of agricultural
labourers was held in the boys' schoolroom on
Saturday evening, to ascertain the, result of the
resolutions passed at the meeting held on the 7th
inst., a printed copy of which was sent to each
employer in the district. Mr. Win. Kneeshaw again
acted as chairman. It was aicertaieel that
several masters had 'model to the advance of
wages demanded by the men, but objected to any
alteration of time. Some other masters refused to
give the advance; in those cases the men generally
have struck work. A teaolution was passed
pledging those who have obtained the advance to
do all in their power to assist those who are still
holding out. There appeared a general divosition
to meet the masters in a conciliatory spirit with
respect to overtime and shorter hours on Saturday,
if the advance of wages were freely conceded.
The men were in capital spirits, it being well
known that work is abundant in the district.
DUNDEE..—The Dundee tailors have struck for
shorter hours and increased wages.

articles.text:
ACT.

DEPUTATION TO THE HOME SECEE.

TARY.

On Thursday afternoon last, a deputation
waited upon Mr. Bruce, at the Home-office, to
submit a memorial that some repeal or altera-
tion should be made in the Criminal Law Amend-
ment Act. Mr. A. M'Donald, the chairman, and
Mr. G. Howell, the secretary of the Trades Union
Congress Parliamentary Committee, were pre-
sent ; as were also Mr. Geo. Potter, Mr. Leigh, and
several other of the leading representatives of
Trades Unions. The deputation was introdheed
by Mr. Mundella, M.P. for Sheffield.
Mr. Mundolla said that the gentlemen present,
who formed a Parliamentary Committee, had
been appointed at a meeting which they held in
January last, to draw up a memorial for the con-
sideration of the right hon. gentleman, the Home
Secretary. In introducing them he (Mr. IMun-
della) was not called upon to express any feelings
of his own in the matter, although they might
be known; and the gentlemen present would give
every explanation necessary, and furnish docu-
ments to support their memorial. Mr. Bruce had
expressed his willingness, he believed, to endeavour
to repeal any law which acted unfairly on any
class, as it was not the wish of the Government for
a clause in this Act to work prejudioislly ; awl he
had also stated in another place the undesirability
of oppressive punishment being inflicted on any
class, whether belonging to Trades Unions, or
otherwise. He would now ask Mr. Howell to
read the memorial and to supply any information
necessary.

Mr. Howell, after thanking the right hon.
gentleman for receiving the deputation, then read
the following

MEMORIAL TO THE RIGHT HONOURABLE HENRY
AUSTIN BRUCE,

Her Majesty's Principal Secretary of State fpr the
Home Department.
Sin,—We, the undersigned, the officers of the
Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee,
appointed at the Fourth Annual Trades Union
Congress held in Nottingham during the second
week in January of this year, and representing, by
delegation, Trades Unionists to the number of
over 375,000, and indirectly nearly as many more,
beg most respectfully to lay before you, a 3 the
representative of the Government for the Home
Department, the feelings of our constituents with
reference to the Criminal Law Amendment Act.

together with some considerations as to its
operation, so far as it has been already invoked by
the employers as an instrument of oppression in
the soveral oases, amongst others, hereinafter
mentioned.

First.—Your memorialists most respectfully
submit that the new law called the Criminal LAW
Amendment Act is founded on the pre-supposition
of criminal intentions, on the part of that large
section of her Majesty's subjects known as trades
unionists ; this, we humbly submit, i in itself an
act of injustice, caused by an imperfect knowledge
as to the aims, objects, and working of those
societies called Trades Unions.

, Secondly.—We submit to your consideration
also, that any act of violence a3ainst Noun or
property, either by an individual or by conf'.•.ina-
tion, is fully met by the Common 1...tw or :Walllt,
and by the General Statute and Common
such as are applied to the other subjects of the
realm; and that, therefore, the applieation of
special legislation to acts committed by that nume
rous and influential section of our artiz an classes
which your metnorialists represent, cannot but be
regarded by thorn as a special wrong, inasmuch as
they are as incapable as any other portion of her
Majesty's subjects of openly or secretly violating
either the letter or the spirit of the laws of the
land.

Thirdly.—Your memorialists most respectfully
call your attention to the cases which have been
already tried under this new law, and we submit
that great injustice and cruelty have been inflicted
by the way that the law has been interpreted and
enforced. With regard to the oases of violence
'which have occured, we have an word of apology
to offer. These, we all admit, are and should be
punishable. Reports of these cases, taken from
the newspapers, will be found appended to this
memorial (and, no far as we can learn, the record
is a complete one), and we would more especially
draw your attention to the Bolton case, both as it
was presented to the magistrates, and on the hear-
ing of the appeal before the Recorder. All the
other cases that have occurred in which violence
was used, wore, in point of law, assaults.
Fourthly.—We have further to submit that even
were the law found to be necessary in order to
reach and punish a class of offences not clearly
within the pale of the Common Statute and
Criminal Law, that, nevertheless, there are either

no definitions where definitions ought to be, or
that the definitions are so vague and uncertain that
cases of great hardship have arisen, and are likely
yet to arise from these defects, other than those
mentioned as having already occurred under the
working of this exceptional and class-made Act.
Your Memorialists, therefore, most °ernes
pray that her Majesty's Government will bring
a short Bill to repeal pris Act, or they will support
the repeal of this law if the repeal be moved by
an independent Member of the House, which, if
it could bo proven to have ever been necessary for
the purpose of retraining or punishing acts of
exceptional violence, is certainly necessary no
longer; and which so long as it shall remain on
the Statute Book, will ever be regarded as ob-
noxious, and will, therefore, be a came of discon-
tent to all those who, though Unionists, and as
such specially legislated against in the Act re-
ferred to, are, nevertheless, as law abiding as any
other portion of her Majesty's subjects. So long
as this Act remains on the Statute Book, the
Trades Union Act, with all its advantages, will
remain inoperative for good. But if the absolute
repeal of the Act be deemed at present impracti-
cable, we pray for snob improvemeat to be made
in its provisions as will prevent the recurrence of
the abuses such as have been enumerated and
pointed out as having arisen in connection with _
the operations of this Act.
And your Memorialists, 8:c.
Signed,
ALEXANDBIL McDoram, Chairman .
WILLIAM ALLAN, Treasurer.
GEonos iIowELL, Secretary.
Trades Union Congress Parliamentary Committee.

In handing the memorial, Mr. Howell said, it
was also accompanied by a complete record of
cases that hail been heard since the passing of the
Act, so far as the committee bad ' been able to
ascertain; they had presented them just as they
had appeared .in the newspapers, in order that
they might not be thought to have tampered with.
them while condensing the reports. The deputation
repreaented a verylarge section of the trades unions.
They knew the Government would have greatdifilcul-
ties iL effecting a repeal of this Act, but they at pre-
sent only asked for an amendment in one or two of
the clauses, or that the act be restored to the same as
it was before coming from ad. House of Lords.
Had it passed as it was than, it wodil 'have been
advantageous. The word "besetting" was not
clearly defined, and although he was not able to
suggest another wind, ho did not think the ono in
question an appropriate one. The word beset-
ting " suggested criminality on the
.part of the
werkman. Another objection. was to the word
"coerce," which they also felt was liable to be
misconstrued by, those who, had the decision of
these cases. In answer to Mr. Bruce, Mr. Howell
said they had furnished the reports of nineteen
eases in the documents presented, hut they did not
include one of any act of violence. Some had
occurred, at Gateshead and , some at Newcastle.
There -was also one at Haunnersraitb, which had
not been decided. The memorialists hoped the
Government would take this into their early consi-
deration,, for there was no. redress but for those
who. could. appeal against the decisions. Appealing
was most expensive, and could only be instituted
by societies which ~had large funds, and those
societies. which had appealed had been auseessful.
In' conclusion he trusted the Government, through
the bon. gentleman, would give it Their considera,
tion.

Mr. MgDonald said he had no wish to repeat
what had been so clearly laid down by Mr.
Howell. He would wish it understood, however,
that the association with which he was connected
had no desire to harass the Government, and if

,

WORK AND WAGES IN CANADA. .

A lecture was delivered on Tuesday night,
ThohniC COnnolly, who hits *specially
visited North America to obtain information
on the subject—" On Canada as a Home for
Working Men." It was given in the new
Cowed. Hall, Agricultural Hall, and IV. T.
M'Cullagh Torrens, Esti: -M.P., .one of the
members for Finsbury, took the chair.
The Chairman, in opening the proceedings,
said they were assembled there on that oeca-
skin to hear from Mr. Connolly: the; resu It o
his observations in a regent visit paid by him
to Canada and the United States. They would
be mainly directed towards, the elucidation of
the question of labour—of all questions the
most important of the present day. From
personal knowledge of his able, witty, and
discerning friend, ho could say there were few
people' he, for, one, would sooner listen to, to
gain instruction and edification on the subject.
.Connolly, was warmly applauded. He
said that when he came home from America
an idea entered his mind to the effect thut he
would write a leiiture on what lie saw. in that
country. He did so, and onlooking over it the
I thought struck him that he might be able to
speak as well as write one, and it Was in that
capacity he appeared before them that even-
ing to tell a plain, unvarnished tale of what
his opinions and feelings were, as derived
from observation and experience: It was said
that the sun never sets on our Empire; that
the morning drum never ceases to beat; that
our commerce was to be found in every sea
, and in every clime ; the people raised 70
' millions of money with as much ease as a man
could procure as many pounds; and yet, after
all, one in every twenty-three of the population
were paupers, .and misery and distress pre-
vailed throughout the land. Their territory
in Canada, from the Atlantio to the Pacific,
contained as much -good' land as Would give
200 acres to every family in this country.
Two provinces, such as Ontario alone, -Would
feed the population of the United Kingdom;
and in the neighbourhood of the St. Lawrence
were the most fertile Valleys and the richest
land on the continent of America; and it was
'a sad thing to see so much misery in this
country, with apparently no remedy for it.
Money was not so much required by an
emigrant as a strong arm and a firm will;
and- very many of those whose descendants
were now in' a prosperous condition \tont to
Ontario and Other' parts of Canada with
scarcely a dollar' in their possession.
Indeed, in his own experience, he never
knew a man to do well in that ,country until
'he had lost all the, money in., his possession,-
'(a laugh) —and had to betake hiniaelito agri-.
cilltural pursuits. In, the province of. Ontario
the:authorities were prepared to give 160 acres
rent free for ever of some of the finest land in.
the world. Lot it be remembered that it did
not require . an ,experience of farming to
succeed at it in .Canada, for he had known
many artisans who became, after a short time,
very good farmers. There , was another ad-
vantage in Canada, and indeed in the United
State, and that was, that food Was ahundt,int ;,
that every man and his family had enough to
support them, and, there was hone of that
wretchedness which unhappily prevailed so
much at home. And nowadays railways were
Opening ury the resources of the country mall
directions, The railroad from the Atlantic to'
the Pacific, which Waa calculated to cost 160
millions of dollars, Would in a short time be
completed, and at present there were railways

articles.text:
SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO TRE WORKING CLASSES OF GREAT BRITAIN.

grea)

FULOW WORKMEN,—
The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Miell to
the judgment of the Rouse of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
SUCCeB4. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature t
apply the principle of that measure to the est of
the United Kingdom. He was met with the objee-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—winch
indeed it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishment
of the State-Church iii Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Mall, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adopt it.
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the Liberation
of Religion from State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro.
flounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, after the broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their hoxest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
loader of the Liberal party in the Rouse of Com-
mons' and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Mon, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone, as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour of, or against, the Dis-
endowment and Disestablishment of the State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland; but also,
and perhaps especially, with a view to the
return of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, whensoever that may take
place. The Rouse of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a faithful and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Commons,
each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
• These, then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated-
1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of conscience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.
2. They aro of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the. United Kingdom has
been disestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the United
Kingdom
3. They are persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to accomplish the task for which it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Trial People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed Protestantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the .British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconformist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

6. 'rho immense revenues of the English and
Scottish Establishments alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance; because
those revenues, though they common property
of the whole nation, are. distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, of the'
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries
and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Dieitaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part fulls to those who have the few cat
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations. ,
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy arc neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they responsible to, the People.. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affect their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Ifence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on the other.
7. The Establishment is a source of national
weakness, because it divides tbe nation into two
hostile parties. It prevents good men uniting, as
. they otherwise might unite, in works of philan-
thropy and in movements for social reform. It
thus carries a mischievous sectarianism into almost
all the affairs of life.
Such are the questions which the Committee of
Working Men commend to the. serious consideration
of their fellow workmen throughout the country.

In order to ascertain and give effect to their views,
Branch Committees will be formed, and meetings
held, in all the large towns. It is hoped, and believed,
that the practical result will be that, after this
-t question has been submitted to the electors,
when it is next debated in the House of Commons,
Mr. Miall will be in a position to give to Mr.
Gladstone's challenge a satisfactory and decisive
answer.—We are, on behalf of the Working
Men's Committee, Yours faithfully,
Li-NORGE HOWELL (Chairman).
DANIEL Guma (Treasurer).

'We do not agree with Sir CHARLES

The principle of Republicanism, as opposed

national life, not by individual logic. Re-

articles.text:
THE SPECTitTO.R AND THE .WAStr-

INOTON TREATY.

Tim Spectator last week, in discussing the
American answer to Lord GRANVILLE'S
"friendly communication," objected to a sug-
gestion of the Times, to the effect that if the
Treaty be again remitted to Washington for
readjustment, the same Commissioners be not
appointed for that purpose. The Spectator
thinks otherwise, and justifies our Commis-
sioners in regard to the blunder by which we
are nowperplexed, on the ground that not they,
but Mr. GLADSTONE and his Government at
borne were responsible for it. At the same
time our modest weekly contemporary throws
out the suggestion, "that a shrewd, practical
lawyer added to the commission would cer-
tainly strengthen it."
We have nothing to say against "shrewd,
practical lawyers." They are a class wise in
their generation, and know how to look after
themselves. What we want to point out, how-
ever, is the gross insult to the American
people and Government such a suggestion
contains, Our Commissioners have blundered,
and we want to place the responsibility else-
where. To say that it was the Government,
not the Commissioners, does not mend the
matter, as it only involves both parties
without exonerating either. If the Com-
m. lasion.rs sent the Treaty from Washington
to London with the blunder in it, and the
Government assented to it without detecting
this blunder, other parties are criminated,
but nobody is excused. If we are to believe
that those who acted for us noted wisely
and rightly, there is no other possible inference
but that the men who acted for the Washing-
ton Government conducted their ease with
chicanery and with dishonourable reticence.
Bence it is suggested that if the negotiations
be ro-opened a shrewd practical lawyer should
be added on our side--on the principle, we
suppose, of seting a thief to catch a thief. Ours
are high-minded honourable men; theirs,
not being aristocratic swells; cannot lift them-
selves to, a high-ugnded performance of duty.

We therefore must let ourselves down to
them, and protect ourselves by a clever petti-
fogger who will be able to guard us from
further cunning omissions or insertions.
The idea may be practical and useful, but
it may be fairly asked whether or not the
Americans can regard, it otherwise than as
an insult—not perhaps eonseiously given, but
still an insult. Our newspapers are, we dare
say, very clover, and frequently throw out
ideas worth attending to, but it can scarcely
be denied that occasionally they arc charac-
terised by a superciliousness and folly which
are neither creditable to them nor wholesome
for the nation.
THE CASE WITH AMERICA.

WE have at length soma means of judging
how the United States intend to shape their
attitude towards us. Unless forecast be much
mistaken, it signifies reason and peace, not
arrogance and war. The Ministers, who in our
two Houses of Parliament, gave so much infor-
mation on the last communication from the
other side as the Cabinet deemed expedient
and consistent with the present situation, have
not fully enlightened the anxious public, but
they have said enough to allay apprehension,
perhaps to encourage hope. The tone and
bearing of both wits molt as to intimate calm
trust in the progress of correspondence as not
even exciting, still less irritative. In point of
firmness, perhaps, the PRIME MINISTER, as
beseemed his place, seemed to surpass some-
what the FOREIGN SECRETA.RY ; but Mr.
GLIDSTONE, as well as Earl GRANVILLE, let
fall expressions fairly, and therefore safely
leading to the anticipation, of a peaceful result
in the end.

The reply from Washington is repr c-
anted as amicable in terms. This, after
what we know of American diplomacy, is
not much. Nor is it concealed from us, that
the substance of the document sent through
General SCHENCK, falls too far short of the
views entertained by our Ministers. They do
not tell us that it demands or requires or calls
for a rejoinder, but that it "invites " one, this
convenient French word being observably used
by both the PREMIER and the EA.AL, JJy our
neighbours this polite form of expression is
often employed where a determination to com-
pel those who receive the " invitation " is in
the minds of the men that give it. We may
venture to infer, howover,/that, on this occa-
sion, the phrase Would not have been used in
concert, had not the tone of the communication
to which it refers been both free from embitter-
ment and in some degree positively concilia-
tory. _ _

At the same time, it has not been thought
proper to lay the corresi)ondence before Parlia-
ment. In this respect, the two Houses are
only treated as President GRANT has treated
Congress. We can readily conceive what
might have been the consequences on
the other side, had a premature pub-
lication taken place. Portions of the
transatlantic press have foreshown us the
sentiments that might have been easily in-
flamed into one of those devouring fires which
nothing but blood is equal to quench. What-
ever, therefore, we may justly think of the
right of papers to be acquainted with proceed-
ings as well as with measures in which they
are nationally concerned, it is better that such
a conglomerate as the population of the United
States should wait till it can be announced
from Washington that satisfaction has been
gained and peace preserved, than that the
risk should be incurred of creating an un-
governable outcry of the whole sum of al-
leged damage, direct and indirect, immediate
and consequential, by disclosing the state of
the negotiations at a stage and under circum-
stances when a less insisting tone as to com-
pensating claims of an overweening order
might dangerously disappoint the greedy ex-
pectations raised by unreasonable and un-
warrantable demand. -

Before this sheet can seethe light, the re-
joinder of the English Government will be
known in substance at the White House in
Washington. Let us hope that it will be alike
firm and temperate, and that it will be pacific
in its influence ; if not decisive in immediate
effect. In the meantime we can but reproduce
and ponder the few words which have fallen
from the lips of our own Ministers. Earl

GRANV/LLE admits that the whole matter re-
mains fraught with anxiety, in which the
QUEEN'S advisers find themselves still sharing.
On the one hand, they earnestly desire to
maintain the Treaty; on the other they feel
the very grave responsibility which lies upon
them to maintain the dignity and the interests

of this country." The statement of Mr.

GLADSTONE in the House of Commons COMeS
to the same points of desire and duty, though
with more largeness and more explicitness.
The American reply is described as couched in
courteous, and even friendly, terms. In
substance, however, it does not come up
to the views of those • for whom it was
written. Par, nevertheless, from being
conclusive and ultimate, it not simply contains
that which gives occasion for rejoinder, but,
as the PREMIER says, appears to anticipate
as well as to invite one. In declining to lay
the papers before the House, Mr. GLADSTONE
rests the refusal upon the simple grounds of
inconsistency with the public interest to
produce an "incomplete correspondence."
With respect to the irresponsible suggestion
of Mn. Disnem, that it would be necessary
for Parliament to deliberate upon the
Treaty with a view to some decisive
issue before the end of April, his answer
is, that it would be premature at the present
stage to assume a necessary break in the
interval to the proceedings contemplated
under that instrnment. In venturing to
expect that ,the two Houses would follow the
example of forbearance set by Congress, Mr.
GLADSTONE referred to the peculiar authority
of the Senate in the ratification of Treaties as
constituting an additional reason why the
patiently waiting attitude of that Chamber
should weigh with our own Houses of Legis-
lature. At the end, the PREMIER
comes to the same point as the FOREIGN
Seenwr.tnr. "While on the one hand," ob-
serves Mr. GLADSTONE, "we shall continue
most anxious to maintain and, carry out the
Treaty of Washington, on the other hand we
shall, .1 trust, be found not to fail in that sense
of the state and nature of the ease which the
honour of this country may demand." It re-
quires, we confess, some degree of sanguine
ingenuity to extract the rays of hope out of
so vague, indefinite, and cloudy a sentence;
yet we also will cherish the trust, and persist
in the prayer, that the world may not be
called to look upon so dreadful a calamity as
hostile encounter between two great States,
peopled mainly b! men, women, and children
of the same faith, language, and blood.

TIIE MISTERS AND SERVANTS
WAGES BILL.

THE most forbearing and long, suffering
members of the Liberal party cannot conceal
from themselves the"faot that the Home De-
partment in Government legislation has not
prospered under Mr. 0 LA.Dsrown's Premiership.
Instead, however, of snaking a change as to
its head, he has found in the Member for
b'troud a zealous and promising lieutenant for
unfortunate Mr. Bnuon. In several emer-
gencies last session Mr. WINTERBOTIUr came
to his rescue; in the present he seems to be
taking care of some of the business of the
office from the beginning. The Masters and
Servants Wages Bill may seem to great poli-
ticians a small affair. It is, however, so far
as it goes, a matter of real importance; and
we observe with interest the way in which
the UNDER-SECRETARY proposes to carry it
through. If the Bill be small, the evil it is
designed to remedy is great enough. It is, in
fact, either a Bill for the surer prevention of
Truck, or one in which we are asked to place
our trust as having that end in view. Exoept
among a raeanly.avaricious class of employers
and a grasping order of underlings, the method
of paying wages in goods of dubious quality
at high prices, and on which the masters
themselves do not disdain to make a profit,
while those to whom they delegate the man-
agement not unfrequently grow comparatively
rich by the extortion, Truck is held in abhor-
rence and abomination. It has in it some of
the worst elements of two things which are
exceedingly vile, degrading, debasing, and
dishonourable—slavery and robbery.
Truck, at all events, is as illegal as either theft
or slave owning But hitherto Ao tremor o

9

Acts of Parliament has had ingenuity enough
to frame a Statute whioh would not be evaded
by lawyerlike craft hired by avaricious greed.
It remains to be seen, whether Mx. WINTER.
BOTIILII, the representative of a manufacturing
borough, if not personally or relatively con-
nected with manufacturing interests, and,
withal, a learned as well as an honourable
gentleman, has succeeded in doing what no
one before him has had the honesty or the
good fortune to achieve. We need not at
present dwell upon the shame and disgrace
which Truck reflects upon the employers who
allow or have recourse to it, or upon thelard-
ships and evils which it brings upon or occa-
sions to the men on whom it is imposed like
a yoke of bondage. That it undermines all
thrift, and destroys all sense of independence,
besides robbing men of their earnings and en-
snaring them in improvidence, wastefulness,
and ruinous intemperance—all these things
are well known, and cannot be denied, except
by those in whose factories and workshops the
practice is unknown.
What the men and their true friends want
to know is, whether Mr. WINTERBOTHLM'S
Bill is likely to'make the statutory prohibition
of Truck an interdict not to be evaded, and,
if violated, sure of real and felt punishment
to the criminals, Well, it avowedly provides
that all wages should be paid in money, with-
out any deduction or the imposition of any
condition as to the manner in which
suoh money shall be spent. With re-
spect to the time when the earner's claim on
his employer becomes good and valid, and is
to be met by positive and actual payment, the
Bill seems to be equally express, though
not, it may be, equally satisfactory. When it
is proposed to enact that wages shall be due
from day to day, or at intervals of less than a day,
something even more in accordance with strict
right than weekly payments appears to have
been secured. But when the Bill proceeds to
talk of ten per cent. standing over as unpaid
balance, which the employer may hold in
reserve for as long as four weeks together, the
measure assumes the aspect of a see-saw betwixt
master and man, for which no cause in plain
reason, utility,. or equity between the parties,
occurs to the unsophisticated mind. The pro-
visions of the Bill, that wages shall not be
paid either in a public) house or in any other
place where goods are on sale to the workmen
receiving the wages, are on the face of them
good, provided always that the preventive and
primitive machinery be equally good and
efficient.

When, however, we are assured that the
Bill is a "strong Bill,'' we become naturally
solicitous to know that the whole apparatus
for making it operative is entitled to that
character. It is, therefore, to be hoped, that
the myriads whom it interests, will not wisely
satisfy their own minds by a searching scrutiny
of every clause, but that those who load
them will take care to avail themselves of
the sharpest legal aceumen in ordbr to make
certain of no secret door being left ajar,
at which cunning evasion may escape from
within the high wall by which it is supposed
to have been shut in, Have, for instance,
the Inspectors, whether of mines or of fac-
tories, heretofore done their appointed work
so very effectually, that the practical business
of suppressing Truck can be trusted wholly in
their hands? The Home Office has already
been told that the penalties are totally in-
sufficient. Mere flue will never restrain
extortion, dictated ever by avarice; but a
few months' quiet meditation in a prison,
or the simple prospect of it, might have A
wonder-working effect.
