; let them sink personalities,
and above all things, bring an absorbing devotion
to the cause they espouse, bearing in mind the
following words of Emerson,---" Every great and
commanding Movement in the annals of the world
is the triumph of enthusiasm."
The bell was vrell tilled, and the lecture was
received with repeated applause.
On the motion of Ur, Pasemore Edwards, a
vote of thanks was accorded- by acclamation to
Captain Mamie for his lecture.

articles.title: WEEK'S NEWS.
articles.text:
THE WEEK'S NEWS.

The execution of Edward Roberts for the
murder of Ann Merrick took place en Monday
morning at Oxford on the old scaffold (used on
former occasions when public executions were
held), in a retired spot were held in the Castle
grounds, just under St. Georges Tower. There
were only 13 persons present, including Calera ft,
who arrived at Oxford the previous night.
The culprit received the Holy Communion in
the chapel at about half-past 7, from the hands
of the gaol chaplain, the Rev. John Thorp.
After the wretched man had shaken hands
with his gaolers, to whom he spoke last, the
bolt was drawn, and the culprit expired
immediately. He had preserved. great com-
posure during the trying ordeal, for which he
seemed fully prepared. In accordance with
the Act of Parliament, all those present signed
a declaration that judgment of death had been
executed, and the black flag was raised on the
timer over the lodge. A coroner's inquisition
afterwards sat on the body, which was even-
tually interred in a grave in the old ohurch-
yard.

The remains of William Murphy, the anti-
Roman Catholic lecturer, were interred on
Monday afternoon at Key-hill Cemetery, Bir-
mingham. The police authorities feared a
disturbance; but, owing to the precau-
tions taken, the manifestations of hostility,
though alarming at one time, were kept within
limits, and no serious accident occurred.

A meeting was held on Monday at King's
Lynn, in order to found a Convalescent Home
at Huntstanton, within a few miles of the
Norfolk residence of the Prince and Princess
of Wales, who, it is hoped and
will take a special interest in the under-
taking.

A death-blow has been given by the New
York Senate to the Erie Railway Ring, in
finally passing the bill for repealing the Clas•
silioatiou Act.

M. There' latest interview with the Com-
mission on the Budget has raised a suspicion
that the duties on raw material may again be
made a Cabinet question.

Notice has been given by the French go-
vernment of the denunciation of the Treaty of
Commerce. In Brussels, and elsewhere on
the Continent, reports continue to. be circu-
lated that some of the Treaty Powers meditate
a retaliator), policy. Joint action of a remon-
strative kind is being, it is said, concerted by
the four principal Powers interested.

Ex-General Cremer of the Commune, has
been accused by Admiral Saisset of having
offered to sell to him a Communist prisoner of
distinction—no less a man than General
Chauzy. The price was to be so much hard
cash and confirmation of Cremer's military
rank. The Admiral has been called out, and,
strangely enough, he finds that Ohanzy is to
be his antagomst's second. There are hopes
of a paoiflo settlement.

Jules Simon will not allow his scheme of
primary instruction to be mangled by the
commission which lately rejected its most
essential' provisions. lie has answered that
he will maintain it "textually."

French finance is again on the carpet, and
M. Thiers has taken the Budget of 1872 under
his special protection. It encountered a ve-
hement assault front the economists; one
Deputy threatening a series of amendments
which would cut it down by a quarter million
of francs. The President declared that there
was no increase except in the war estimates,
and these had been enlarged for the purpose
of " creating an army which should not be an
illusion."

At a meeting of the Board of Works it was
decided that the Board would not be justified
in paying £40,000 for the laud reclaimed from
the Thames lunhankment, according to the
terms of the bill introduced into the House of
Commons by the Chancellor of the Exchequer;
but that they might pay an annual rental
for it, or the capitalised value of such rettal.

Statistics in reference to dipsomania, or
habitual drunkards, were afforded to a cora-
mittoo of the House of Commons by Mr.
Mould, superintendent of the Manchester
Royal Asylum. Amongst other facts, it was
stated that about 15 per cent. of certificated
lunatics were cured, and about 7 per cent. of
the dipsomaniacs.

Au important question arose in the Bank-
ruptcy Court, in reference to the petition of
Mr. T. Clapham, of Leeds, as to whether cer-
thin fully paid-up shares in the Leeds. Park
Estate Building and Investraent Company
should be transferred to the creditors at their
full value. The Registrar decided that the
term "composition" in the Act referred to
money, and. 'that shares could not fairly be
forced on ereditors against their will, as they
did not know what 4ability lay behind them.

The Tichborne Bonds were sold on the Open
Stock Exchange last week at £3 the £lOO.

A scheme is now being arranged in Paris
for testifying the gratitude of the French
nation to England for the succour sent to the
victims of the war. No less than 116 com-
munes have undertaken to co-operate with
the Paris Committee. It is intended to dis-
tribute among thetn sheets of vellum, adorned
with their respective municipal arms. These
are to be inscribed with the names of the
representative inhabitants. When collected,
the sheets will be handsomely bound in
volumes, which will be placed in an orna-
mental cabinet and forwarded to the Mansion
House.

A patriarchal Wiltshire farmer, who died
at the age of ninety-five, and at eighty-six
could lift a saok of corn with one hand, made
a will dividing his property, of some £30,000
amongst his children and grandchildren.
This was disputed by his eldest son, lately
returned from Australia, in the Probate
Court; but the will was pronounced valid,
without any order as to costs.

At Bow-street, a country girl, aged 19, was
sent for trial on the strange charge of stealing
a child of a sergeant of the Royal Engineers.
Through the publicity given by the press, the
girl and child were traced to the casual ward
of St. George's-in-the-East. Her defence was
that the child had been "given to her."

John Kirby, charged with having caused
the death of a woman of bad character named
Crew, was on Monday brought up before the
Thames Police magistrate, and committed for
trial on an indictment for manslaughter. The
evidence, which has already been reported,
was identical with that given before the
Coroner.

M. Tillers visited the Chateau of St. Cloud
on Sunday to ascertain whether or not the
building was set fire to by means of petroleum.
Ile found that the cellars and foundations are
the only parts of the building which remain in
such a state as to be made use of.

The evidence taken by the Afegcora Commis-
sion is published. It fills a folio volume of
7(36 pages.

By direction of the Lords of the Admiralty
the usual notice has been issued at Chatham,
stating that all hired workmen will be dis-
charged on the 31st March, and those required
re-entered on the Ist April , but this discharge
is not in any way to affect the gratuities to
which the men may have become entitled
through long service. This discharge is merely
of a formal character, as the men are always
re-entered,

The Worshipful Company of Merchant
Taylors has granted a sum of fifty guineas to
the funds of the Camden Sohool for Girls.

The V ioe.rago of Shotteswell, near Kineton,
has become vaoant by the death of the Rev.
Alfred Hooke, M.A. it is worth .C2OO a year,
and is in the gift of Colonel North, M.P.

The Earl of Sheffield has presented the Rev.
Humphrey A. Slack, M.A., curate of Know-
stone, to the chapelry of Danehill, near !Mc-
field, Sussex. The Bishop of Bath and Wells
has instituted the Rev. Thomas George Hor-
wood, M.A., formerly curate of Heywood, to
the rectory of Crotcombe, near Wells.

One of the Bombay papers says that the
"celebrated Theresa Longworth, alias Mrs.
Yelverton, alias Lady Avon/non), arrived at
Hong Kong a short while ago for the purpose
Of giving public readings there. She has come
from San Francisco after an American tour.
From China she will visit Australia."

The I)ttridee Advertiser says the boy named
William George Drummond Steuart, who was
alleged to be the son of the late Major Steuart,
and who claimed to be the heir to the Murthly
estates, has just died, after an illness of
fourteen days. His death puts an end to a
litigation the result of which had been looked
forward to with much interest.

Le Nord says that the collar of the Order
of the Golden Fleece which was sent by King
Amadeus of Spain to the Comte do Flandre is
the identical collar which was worn by
Christopher Columbus' and with which he
was invested, with the Order, by Ferdinand
and Isabella, in honour of the *discovery of
America.

A Times Paris telegram states that the
Special Parliamentary Commission has
rejected the proposal to authorise the Bank
of France to receive accounts current bearing
Interest, contrary to the announcement which
had been made.

Monday was the 24th anniversary of the
birth of the Princess Louise. Thursday the
21st inst., was the first anniversary of the
marriage of her Royal Highness to the Mar-
a Lorne.

The denunciation of the Treaty of Com-
merce with France has been communicated to
her Majesty's Government.--Foreign-office,
March 15, 1872.

On the 15th inst., at Hanley, a young
woman named Hill, in business as a grocer
and beerseller, admitted a charge accusing her
of the murder of her illegitimate child.

The Committee on Pardons has rejected the
appeals of Preau de Vedel Questel, and Girard,
who are under sentence of death for complicity
in the assassination of the hostages.

lho Duke do Montpensier will shortly
address a letter to those Spaniards in the pro-
vinces who offered him their support for ob-
taining a seat in the Cortes, stating that he
declines offering himself as a candidate.

Mr. Tennyson is engaged on a poem on the
illness of the Prince of Wales, which will
appear shortly.

Mr. Swinburno has written a poem on the
death of Mazzini, whioh will appear in one of
the April magazines.

The Lord Mayor presided on Tuesday even-
ing at a public meeting of the Church
Defence Institution, at the Bridge-house
hotel.

There was a thoroughly representative
gathering at the dqjeliner given by the Mayor
of Portsmouth, to Lord Northbrook on Mon-
day. His lordship, in response to the toast of
his health, spoke of the difficulty of legislating
for a country like India, with its masses o
peorde of different religions and various cusf
tome; and dwelt upon the necessity of caution
in dealing with the interests, the wishes, and
the prejudices of the numerous races owning
her Majesty's sway. Amongst the other
speakers were Lord Tenipletown, Sir Rodney
Mundy, Mr. Cowper-Temple, M.P., Mr. Stone,
ALP., and Mr. Bonham-Carter, M.P.

The nomination for West Cumberland will
take place at Cookermouth on Tuesday next.
Should no vacancy arise in the meantime, this
election will once more make the House of
Commons complete. Beverley, Bridgwater,
Cashel, and Sligo having been disfranchised,
the total number of members is now 632.

The Joint Committee of Lords and Commons
upon the subject of railway amalgamation
again met on Monday, the .President of the
Board of Trade in the chair. The evidence
taken was adverse to the proposed amalgama-
tion between the London and. North Western
and Lancashire and Yorkshire Companies.

A man named Fitzgerald, of 125, Great
Portland-street, "gentleman," was fined at
Marlborough-street X 5 for eaoh of two assaults
on men, and £2 10s. for an assault on a
woman, whom ho had grossly insulted, besides
£2 Ws. compensation to one of the men.
His friend Edwards, who attempted to rescue
him from the police, was also fined 4.12 10s.

• The Duchess of Cambridge landed at Dover
on Monday afternoon from the London,
Chatham, and Dover Company's steam packet
Wave. Her Royal Highness had travelled
from Hesse Darmstadt via Frankfort, Brus-
sels and Calais, and had left the latter port
shortly after one o'clock. She suffered so
much from sea-sickness and unfavourable
passage, as to be compelled to abandon her
intention of continuing her journey to London
until Tuesday morning.

A lecture was delivered on Monday night at
Reading, by Mr. J. C. Williams, on "Church
Disestablishment." The Mayor occupied the
chair. In the midst of the lecture, the Church
party, who had assembled in strong force,
commencing groaning and singing "God Save
the Queen." The disturbance at length grew
so great that the lecturer had to sit down.
Several gentlemen essayed to speak, but were
stopped by groans. When the chairman
vacated the chair, the Church party formed up
outside the Church, and serenaded the Dis-
senters as they passed out with "God save the
Queen."

From a return which has been published by
the Registrar-General, it appears that during
the 52 weeks of last year, among the rather
more than seven millions of people living in
London and the 19 other large cities of the
United Kingdom furnishing weekly returns,
the birth-rate was equal to 36 per 1,000, and
the death-rate to 27. The birth-rate differed
but slightly from that in the previous year,
while the death-rate showed an increase of 2
per 1,000, In Dublin the rate was 26, in
Edinburgh 27, while in Glasgow it was so high
as 33, which among the English towns was
only exceeded by the rates in Liverpool and
Sunderland. The Census enumeration in
April last showed that the population of
Edinburgh had been considerably under-
estimated in recent years, while it had been
overstated in Dublin. In Dublin the popula-
tion was a 4 but Atationary during the past ten
years.

Her Majesty did Mr. John O'Connor the
honour to inspect his picture of the Interior
of St. Paul's on or during the Thanksgiving
service before leaving Buckingham Palace on
the 14th inst.

The Indian Budget will probably be sub-
mitted to the Legislative Council on the 15th
of April.

In the army estimates, at page 36, £1,260
has been provided for police, for duty with
the force in the field during the autumn
manceuvres.

On Monday, when the Marlborough-street
police magistrate was prepared to resume the
hearing of the charge of fraud against
•the
Secretary of the Free Dormitory Assooiation,
Mr. E. Lewis, his solicitor' read a letter front
him' in which he stated that he was toe un'
well to leave his house. The prosecuting
attorney, however, said that since the lest
examination the defendant had unsuccessfully
endeavoured to compromise the matter in
dispute, and he therefore applied for a warrant
for his arrest. After a short adjournment
facts came to the knowledge of the defendant's
solicitor which decided him on withdrawing
from the case, and a warrant was issued
accordingly.

Shore Ali, the assassin of Lord Mayo, wati
executed on the 11th. It has been ascertained
by the judicial inquiry that he had no con-
federates, and that he committed the crime
simply out of revenge, because he considered
he was unjustly treated. Ever since his
conviction he had determined to murder a
European of high rank. Lady Mayo and her
family on arriving at Suez will leave the
Glasgow, and return to England in the
Admiralty yacht Enchantress, which will also
bring home the remains of the deceased.

If we are correctly informed, the re-organi-
sation of the Secretariat of the Admiralty by
the creation of a new office, that of Naval
Secretary, is among the reforms contemplated
by Mr. Goschen. It is said that Captain Hall,
now at the head of the Control Department,
will be appointed to this post.
Mr. H. F. Chapman (son of Mr. Chapman,
of the firm of Chapman and Hall) has been
elected manager of the Polytechnic Institution
in the place of Professor Pepper, who has
resigned.

Mr. Francis Ellis APTaggart, who was ar
pointed judge of the Marylohone County Court ta
January, died suddenly on Friday last. He was
a son of Mr. Thomas Flower Ellis, who assisted
Mr. John Loycester Adolphus in the produc-
tion of the well-known series of law reports
which appeared under the sanction of their
joint names, and took the surname of
tki,Taggart on coming into possession of sorsa
property.

A special general meeting of the members
of the Hearts of Oak Benefit Soeiety
was held at Exeter-hall, Strand, on Satur-
day' evening last, for the purpose of
electing a treasurer in the room of Mr. James
Corbett, deceased. There was a very largo
attendance. The candidates for the vaeant
office were William Wanless, the present
interim treasurer, and lately the Society's
chief clerk; Mr. R. P. Harvey, and Mr. T.
Feild. The last-named gentleman having
retired, the contest lay between Messrs. Wan
less and Harvey, and In the result Mr. Wan'
less was declared to be elected by a very large
majority. An attempt was thou made to
induce the meeting to alter the rule relating
to the treasurer's salary, with a view to its
permanent increase, but it was resolved to
leave the rule in its present form until the
next annual meeting.

Vice-Chancellor Wicket; on Monday do;
livered an interesting
,judgment in the case m
the Attorney-General and others v. the
Corporation of Batley. The suit was brought
to restrain the Town Council from providing
out of the local rates a gold chain for the Merr'
at a cost of £2OO. His Honour held that the
proposed expenditure was not within the seeP°
of the Muncipal Corporations' Reform Act!
and that a chain was not a necessary Aluneb
of the magisterial position. The amount ill
question, though small, was no objection to-
the interposition of the court, and the injuilc-
tion must certainly be granted.

An application was made to the Court of
Bankruptcy on Monday for a certificate to th°
Speaker of the House of Commons declaring
that Sir W. Russell, M.P. for Norwich, haa not
satisfied the claims of his creditors, althoufth
more than a year had elapsed since the pool
of a resolution for a liquidation by arrangern°
In consequence of the absence of counsel tbo
hearing of the motion was adjourne4 Or a
week.

The banker, Salomon Heine, of Hambarght
has loft his immense fortune to the widow 01
Heine, the poet. The lady is a Frenchwoman)
and immediately subscribed largely to the
Liberaticat Itua.rX4o,ooo.

On behalf of Mr. Frederick Strange, an
application was on Monday made to the
magistrates at Newington, for a spirit licence
for the Surrey-gardens, which for the past ten
years have been occupied by the temporary
St. Thomas's Hospital. Mr. Strange now
proposes to establish theatrical and musical
entertainments, botanical gardens, and a
public menagerie. 'While there are to be
Pyrotechnic displays, there will be a total
absence of bombardment, and the place is to
be closed. throughout Sundays, and at 11
o'clock every night. The licence is strongly
opposed. by many inhabitants of the locality,
the clergy of the rural deanery of Newington,
and the ministers and Members of Noncon-
formist churches in the neighbourhood.

The Meath hounds met at the Marquis of
Ileadfort's seat near Kens, in Ireland, on the
14th inst. Whilst in the act of mounting his
horse, the noble marquis was thrown, and sus-
tained a severe fracture of the collar-bone.

It is believed at the War Office that the
new army offices will be completed on the
"historical site" within two years from the
present time. The extreme unsuitability of
the present buildings in Pall Mall has, it ap-
pears, induced Mr. Cardwell to put pressure
on the Works' Department to hasten the ar-
rangements.

The hothouse intended to contain specimens
of growing cotton plants during the Exhibi-
tion of 1872 is now being built in the West
Annexe' near Prince Albert's-road, by Mr.
F. G. Messenger, of Loughborough. The
plants are being raised, and will be exhibited
by Major R. Trevor Clarke, of Welton-park,
Daventry.

Another of her Majesty's ships has unfor-
tunately met with a disaster, the armour-plated
screw steamer Lord Clyde, 18 guns, Captain
Bythesea, V.C., having got aground on the
north-west coast of the island of Pantellaria,
whither she had proceeded to assist the
stranded ship Roby Castle. Admiral Key
left Malta in the Enohrantress on the 15th
inst., and was followed by the Lord Warden
and the Research, to aid in rescuing the iron-
clad from her dangerous position.

The marriage of the Marquis of Bute with
the Hon. Miss Howard, which had been fixed
for Tuesday, the 16th prox., will take place
in London, and not in Glossop. This change
in the arrangements has been made in order
,to suit the convenience of the numerous
friends of the noble bride and bridegroom
who will be present at the ceremony. Lord
Bute and his bride, it is believed, will leave
London on the afternoon of their wedding-
day and proceed direct to Cardiff Castle.

The following resolution has been sent from
the India Ofßee for publication:—" Resolved
ttnanimously, by, the Secretary of State for
India in Council, that, having regard to the
eminent services rendered by the late Earl of
Mayo, as Viceroy and. Governor-General of
India, to the munificence with which he main-
tained in that office the dignity of the Crown,
and to his death by a deed of violence to which
be was exposed in the discharge of his public
duty, a life annuity of £l,OOO be conferred on
the Countess of Mayo, to be paid out of the
revenues of India; and, further, that there
be paid out of the same revenues the sum of
£20,000 for the benefit of the younger children
of her ladyship and of the into Earl of Mayo."

A few days since a curious discovery was
made in a garden at Twerton, near Bath.
Whilst some men were engaged in excavating
for a sewer they laid bare a stone coffin, which.,
on examination, was found to contain the
skeleton of a man apparently about 40 years
of age. The coffin, which was covered by two
large stones, was found, on its removal being
attempted, to be hollowed from two stones, the
coffin being joined together in the centre. It
Was found at a distance of two feet from the
surface of the ground. The coffin was aft. Lin.
in the interior from head to foot. A number
of nails were in the coffin' which were of such
a pattern as to lead to the supposition that
they belonged to shoes or sandals. The
skeleton was intact, with the exception of tfie
bead, Which appeared to have undergone seve-
rance previous to interment.

Mazzini's ftmeral took place at Genoa on
Sunday. A crowd of 80,000 persons followed
the car, which Was surrounded by the intimate
friends of
.the deceased, by the members of the
municipality of Genoa, deputations from Pisa,
Naples, Venice, &0., numerous representatives
of the Italian and foreign press, and of many
Working Men's Association? and Masonic
lodges. The latter had their bands. Tho
Windows and balconies were Frowded with
Spectators. The funeral procession started at
noon. All the theatres and, cafes were
closed.

The annual meeting of the Iron and Steel
Institute, was held on Tuesday at Willis's
Rooms, Mr. H. Bessemer in the chair. There
was a large attendance of the iron trade.

A public meeting is shortly to be held in
Birmingham to protest against the recent out-
rages on the Jews in Roumania, and to raise
funds on behalf of the sufferers. Mr. John
Bright, in replying to an invitation to be
present, writes as follows :—" Rochdale, March
15th, 1872,—Dear Sir,—l cannot attend the
proposed meeting in the Town-hall. The out-
rages on the Jews, as reported in the newspaper,
are very shocking. How slow the world is to
learn what is just and right in regard to differ-
ences of religious belief I thank you for your
note of invitation, and am truly yours,
JOHN BRIGHT."

At the Manchester Assizes last week, before
Mr. Justice Lush, Thomas Taylor, 58, post-
master of Stalybridge and. actuary to the
savings bank in that town, pleaded guilty to
having embezzled various sums from the
trustees of the bank, amounting in the
aggregate te £6,240. The way in which he
had succeeded in eluding detection for some
years was that he kept a false pass-book; he
took the true pass-book when he went to the
Manchester and Liverpool District Bank,
where the money should have been deposited,
but presented his false pass-book to the
auditors. He was sentenced to seven years'
penal servitude.

Mr. Samuel C. Kline, of Greenville, Wayne
County, Mo., recently having had three
daughters born unto him, straightway wrote
to G-ov. B. Gratz Brown, and promptly re-
ceived the following reply :—" I have received
your letter of Jan. 5, informing me of the large
addition to your family, and inquiring if there
is any State provision for such oases. I regret
to say that there are none, but I shall refer the
matter at once to the representative of your
county, with the request that they present the
case before the Legislature. But allow me,
sir, to tender my individual congratulations,
with the assurance that.you have deserved well
of the country."

The Indian papers contain long accounts of
the funeral ceremonies in honour of the late
Lord Mayo, which took place at Calcutta.
Great sympathy and regret were displayed, it
is said, by all classes. The Calcutta .English-
man says that the ceremonial was no more
piece of official etiquette, such as Gazettes can
order and upholsterers arrange; it was the
natural and simple expression of the sorrow,
stern, solemn, and heartfelt, of an outraged
community.

It having been ascertained that not more than
1,500 or 1,600 volunteers would attend the pro-
posed review at Portsmouth in April next, the
event will in all probability be postponed till
after the harvest, when it is hoped that a much
larger force will assemble.

Sir Stafford Northoote, in a letter acknow-
ledging the receipt of a petition from Ilfra-
combe in favour of international arbitration,
states it to be a principle of which he entirely
approves, though he fears the difficulties which
lie in the way of its general application to be
not inconsiderable.

On the 16th inst., a House of Commons
return was issued, showing the total consump-
tion of sugar for the year ending the 30th of
September, 1871, in breweries. The sugar so
consumed as follows : England: London,
11,991,690 lb.; the provinces, 17,288,499 lb.;
Scotland, 508,472 lb. ; Ireland, 2,712,1021 b.
Total, 32,300,763 lb.

On Monday night an enthusiastic social
meeting of the Irish in Glasgow, favourable to
Home Rule, was hold in the City Hall; Mr.
John Martin, M.P., who was accompanied by
Mr. A. M. Sullivan, presided. Before the
business proper was entered upon, a telegram
in answer to one previously received from
Dublin, was transmitted to that city, declaring
that the inhabitants of Glasgow desired the
liberation of the men, over fifty in number,
now suffering in prison for their love of Ire-
land. Mr. Martin said that holding, as he did,
very moderate opinions, still in view of all
that had been done to Ireland, he could not
condemn the most desperate Fenian that ever
conspired. The day seemed to have come
when all patriotic Irishmen were able to unite
upon the only ground that was honourable to
all parties. "Ireland for the Irish," "Home
Rule," "Repeal of the Union," or "Irish Na-
tional Independence ; " to him all these meant
the same thing substantially, and he was perfectly
ready to adopt any phrase the majority of his
countrymen thought fit. (Cheers.) Mr. Sulli-
van afterwards a dressed the meeting in strong
terms in favour of Home Rule. Such sentiments
as "Our imprisoned and exiled fellow-
oopntrymen," "The memory of the dead,"
and "Ireland in exile," were afterwards sub-
mitted to the meeting.

In the course of some observations at a
public mooting, held in the Commercial-road.,
Lord Shaftesbury, in speaking of the Alabama
claims, advised this country to maintain a
manly and dignified bearing, which would
prevent mischief, and eventually weld the re-
lations between the two countries into a more
solid friendship than had heretofore existed.

At a meeting of the Senatus of St. Andrew's
University, held on Monday 'afternoon, a letter
was read. from Mr. Ruskin, in which that
gentleman resigned any right (real or
imagina4) which he might have to the rector-
ship. Both candidates having now withdrawn,
the University is in a position to proceed
to a new election, which the Senatus fixed to
take place on Thursday, the 28th inst. The
Bev. William Knight, Dundee, was appointed
examiner in mental and moral philosophy to
the University. The office is tenable for three
'years.

Lord Eloho presided over a special meeting
of volunteer commanding officers on Tuesday,
when the difficulties which have arisen in
connection with the proposed volunteer gather-
ing at Brighton on Easter Monday were con-
sidered, and it was resolved that the anticipated
field-day be abandoned. It was stated at the
meeting that it is now too late to make
arrangements for a review either at Dover or
at Portsmouth.

Tuesday, Dr. W. Smith in the chair, it was
unanimoualy resolved to form an association
or the protection of copyright property. Sir
Charles Trevelyan, Mr. !Limes Murray, Mr.
Longman, and Mr. Charles Reade were amongst
the speakers.

On Tuesday, at the meeting of the Commis-
sioners of Sewers, the report of the Finance
and Improvement Committee was adopted,
recommending the payment of £15,000 to the
Dean and Chapter of St. Paul's for the ground
necessary to carry out the contemplated im-
provement in St. Paul's Churchyard. At the
same meeting it was resolved that the carriage-
way of several City thoroughfares should be
paved with asphalt°.

Fifty out of fity-two weeks of the financial
year had been accounted for when the
Treasury receipts were made up on the 16th
instant. At that time the revenue amounted
to £71,775,525, and this was within £640,000
of the whole year's estimate. Excise and
stamps had already exceeded the anticipated
returns of the full twelve months. The total
receipts are four millions and a half in excess
of those of the corresponding period of last
year. The expenditure has been £67,000,942.
On Saturday last the balance in the Bank of
England was £9,250,946.

The number of births in London last week
was 2,443, and of deaths 1,475, the former
having been 45 above, and the latter 209 be-
low the average. The mean temperature was
44.6.

In the ease of two Liverpool steamers whieh
had been seized by the Government under the
Foreign Enlistment Act, and afterwards re-
leased, the Judge of the Admiralty Court on
Tuesday made a decree for compensation, the
law officers of the Crown having declined to
argue the matter.

At the Clerkenwelllice-eourt, the boy
Thompson, charged with having attempted to
poison the Rev. Chichester Reado and his
family, was formally brought up and remanded,
the analysis of the brandy into which the
emetic tartar is alleged to have been plaoed
not having been completed.

On and after the Ist of April third-olass
passengers will be conveyed by all trains upon
the Midland Railway.

According to promise, Tuesday's Journal
Officiel formally announces that the Treaty of
Commerce between France and. Great Britain
has been denounced by the former Power.
The present tariffs are to remain in force
until others have been voted by the Assembly.

It seems that there were no demonstrations
in Paris on Monday, or in any of the large
towns of France, to celebrate the anniversay
of the establishment of the Commune. In
Paris military precautions were taken on a
somewhat extensive scale, and police agents
in private clothes were dispersed throughout
the city. Their services were not, however,
required, as no disturbances took place.

Preau do Yodel, who had been condemned
to death for the murder of M. Gustave Chaudey,
a writer on the Siecle, who was shot during the
rule of the Commune in Paris, was executed on
Monday at Satory. He showed great courage
to the last, declared in a loud voice that he
was innocent, and told the firing party to aim
straight at his heart. Most of the spectators
of the scene wore soldiers.

On Friday a meeting of the West Cumber-
land Liberal Registrar= Association was hold.
at Cockermouth, and a general feeling was ex-
pressed that it was advisable to oppose the
candidature of Lord Muncaster for West
Cumberland. A letter from Sir Wilfrid Law-
son said they must wait for the ballot, but in
the meantime extend their organisation so as
be so ready when the .day for lighting came.
It it now almost certain that Lord Muneaster
will be returned without opposition.

LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

FRIDAY.

It is understood that her Majesty will em-
bark at Portsmouth to-day (Saturday) on board
the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert, Captain
his Serene Highness the Prince of Leningen,
and proceed to Cherbourg, where her Majesty
will disembark, on the way to Baden. Her
Majesty will not:pass through Paris, but will
reach the Paris western station by the circular
railway. _ _

The Sultan is said to be contemplating a
visit to Italy, leaving Constantinople in April,
and proceeding _afterwards to Lyons for the
Exhibition.

Thanksgiving services for therecovery of the
Prince of Wales have been held throughout
Australia. _ _ _

‘• It is finally settled that the Volunteer
Review is to be held, at Brighton on Easter
Monday.
The Lords of the Admiralty have sent an
order to Chatham Dockyard directing that
the usual annual examination of junior
officers of the yard for promotion is not to be
hed. in future, but examinations are to be
held only when there is a vacancy to be
filled up.

At Wigan on Wednesday delegates repre-
senting 39,000 coal miners mot to consider the
Mines Regulation Bill. It was stated by one
of the committee appointed to watch the
progress of the Bill in Parliament that many
points of difference between masters and men
had been settled, and a resolution affirming
the eight hours principle was adopted.
The rumour mentioned in several journals,
that the Government had sent an order to
Toulon to arm three ironclad men-of-war is
completely false.

The statement published by certain journals
that the Spanish Government was prepared to
accept modifications to any existing Treaty of
Commerce, is devoid of foundation. The
Spanish Government will only not in obedience
to the vote of the Cortes, and in order to
maintain the decisions previously adopted,
will refuse to entertain any modifications
proposed with reference to the customs
duties.

A crowded public meeting was held at
Exeter last night, when resolutions condemn-
ing Mr. Morgan's Burials Bills, and calling on
local members of Parliament to oppose it t were
unanimously carried. It was announced that
similar resolutions had been carried at meet-
ings at Barnstaple, Torrington, and Devonport,
and other meetings were to be held. A protest
had also been sent from Cornwall.

A man named Nagle was brought up at
Worship-street on Wednesday, charged with
the manslaughter of one Anne Coney, in a low
court in Spttalfields. The crime, like many
others similar in character, appeared to have
been the result of drink. Pending the
coroner's inquest, the prisoner has been
remanded.

Efforts are being made to transfer the trial
of Mr. Edmonds, who is eb.arged with the
wilful murder of his wife at Newent, from the
Gloucester Assizes to London, on account of
the prejudice and ill-feeling which are alleged
to exist in that county. Mr. Justices Willos
has granted a summons calling upon the pro-
secution to show cause why the indictment
should not be so removed.

Mr. Gatborno Hardy, M.P., on Wednesday
presided over the annual meeting of the
Charity Organization Society, at which an en-
couraging report of its progress was given.
Amongst the speakers were the Marquis of
Westminster, the Rev. J. Martineau, Lord
Etch°, Sir W. Fraser, the Earl of Lichfield,
and Lord Mahon, M.P.

Professor Huxley was on Wednesday put in
nomination for the rectorship of St. Andrew's
University.

A large number of distinguished ladies and
gentlemen, many of whom had expressly
arrived from Paris for the occasion, paid. their
respects to the Emperor and Empress of the
French, and the Prince Imperial, at Chisle-
hurst on Saturday, which was the sixteenth
anniversary of his Imperial Highness's birth-
day. Among the presents made to the Prince
was an inkstand in the form of a bee-l!lvoi of
most elaborate and artistio workmanship, and
which was subscribed for by the children of
Paris.

We learn by Atlantic Cablo that St.
Patrick's Day was celebrated with much
enthusiasm in New York, and that no serious
disturbances occurred.

Last week the total number of paupers in
the metropolis was 120,111, of whom 34,7(30
were in workhouses and 83,331 received out-
door relief. Compared with the corresponding
weeks in the years 1871, 1870, and 1869,
thew figures show a decrease of 27,611,
49,252, and 28,859 respectively. The VAILI
number of vagrants relieved was 843.
